entries.title: NFL’s Jaylen Harrell hospitalised and investigated for assault in car crash
entries.summary: Police in US investigating whether Tennessee Titans defensive end assaulted rideshare driver before collision.
entries.content:
Police in United States investigating whether Tennessee Titans defensive end assaulted a rideshare driver before collision.

Tennessee Titans defensive end Jaylen ‌Harrell has been hospitalised in Florida ⁠after being ⁠involved as a passenger in a rideshare car in what the team have called a “serious” accident.

The Tampa Police Department said in ⁠a preliminary report that Harrell was riding about 8:45am (13:45 GMT) on Friday in the back seat when “he reportedly assaulted the driver while the vehicle ⁠was in motion.”

The driver of the Kia Sorento then swerved, struck a Toyota Highlander and collided with a utility pole, the police report said.

Police investigation under way

Harrell, 24, was thrown from the backseat, hit the windshield and lost consciousness, according ‌to the police report.

Harrell was hospitalised with serious injuries while the rideshare driver, identified as a man in his mid-30s, sustained “minor injuries” and was treated at the scene, according to police. The driver of the Highlander was not injured, the police said.

Detectives are working through the timeline of events in investigating the crash, according ⁠to the preliminary report.

The Titans issued a statement ⁠on Saturday but did not disclose Harrell’s condition or the injuries he had suffered nor did they mention the assault accusation.

Harrell has not played this season after tearing ⁠an ACL in August during the preseason and being placed on the injured reserve list.

“We have been in constant communication with Jaylen’s ⁠family and are still working to gather more ⁠information,” the team said in its statement.

“At this time, Jaylen remains in the hospital and continues to receive care. We ask that Jaylen and his family’s privacy be respected ‌at this time. We will provide an update when appropriate.”

The accident occurred in Tampa, Harrell’s hometown.

The Titans selected the University of Michigan alumnus in the ‌seventh ‌round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He has appeared in 34 games (two starts) and has 38 tackles, seven tackles for a loss and 4.5 sacks.

entries.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts drone, missile as Houthis report attack on Sanaa
entries.summary: Houthi media say several people were injured in an attack on an oil company as Saudi air defences down a drone.
entries.content:
Houthi media say several people were injured in an attack on an oil company as Saudi air defences down a drone.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a drone and a missile launched by the Houthis, while the media affiliated with the Yemeni group reported that at least six people were wounded in an air attack on an oil company’s fuel station in Sanaa.

The Yemen News Agency quoted the spokesperson for the Ministry of Health and Environment, Anis al-Asbahi, as saying on Sunday that Saudi aircraft targeted a fuel station operated by the state-run oil company on 60th Street, “injuring six employees and causing material damage”.

There was no immediate comment on the claim from the Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

Separately, the Saudi-led coalition spokesman, Turki al-Maliki, said the country’s air defences destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh.

Al-Maliki did not provide further details or report any casualties or damage in his post on X.

His statement came hours after he announced that a ballistic missile was intercepted and destroyed as it targeted the country’s western region, on the coast of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia’s western region has key energy infrastructure, including the Yanbu oil terminal, a facility for crude exports, and the Jazan refinery in the far southwest of the country, which borders Yemen.

The Houthis have attacked oil installations in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, along with airports and military sites.

Meanwhile, clashes continue between the internationally recognised Yemeni government forces and the Houthis on several fronts, amid warnings of worsening displacement and food shortages.

Since seizing Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and the internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again this summer when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces launched a counteroffensive last month to recapture territory from the Houthis, but forces allied to the government earlier this month said they would withdraw from areas around the strait and focus on defending Aden.

Analysts say the conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics in Yemen, and it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the US-Israel war on Iran.

Houthi attacks have killed 26 people in Saudi Arabia since September, including 23 in strikes on airports, according to the kingdom’s authorities.

On Thursday, a tower housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund in Riyadh’s financial district sustained damage on several floors in a Houthi attack, authorities said.

A skyscraper belonging to state oil giant Aramco was also damaged in a strike at the beginning of the month.

entries.title: Children in besieged Gaza struggle to find life-saving insulin for diabetes
entries.summary: Insulin and blood glucose testing supplies become increasingly difficult to obtain in war-torn Gaza.
entries.content:
As insulin and blood glucose testing supplies become increasingly difficult to obtain, families say they are being forced to make impossible choices to keep their children alive.

Gaza City, Gaza Strip – When Amir, a nine-year-old with diabetes, began repeatedly vomiting and complaining of severe abdominal pain, his mother, Nahawand, called an ambulance. He was rushed to a hospital in Gaza City and admitted to intensive care, where doctors found a dangerous build-up of acid in his blood due to insulin poisoning.

Nahawand said last week’s hospital admission was the latest and most frightening consequence of a struggle to find enough insulin to keep Amir alive and his blood sugar under control.

Amir was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes when he was just a year old. His mother has to monitor his blood sugar throughout the day and adjust his insulin according to his readings and meals.

Keeping Amir’s condition under control with diabetes medication has become increasingly difficult due to the high cost of insulin caused by Israel’s crippling siege on Gaza and because her husband is out of work.

After months of being unable to find insulin in Gaza City, 39-year-old Nahawand finally managed to obtain supplies brought from Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, only to discover the medicine had expired.

“I cannot afford to buy it. I am unable to buy insulin for my son at all,” she told Al Jazeera.

Before the war, Nahawand said a single insulin pen cost between 25 and 30 shekels (($7.62 to $9.17), or was free through clinics and aid organisations. Now a pen costs between 50 and 80 shekels ($15.29 to $24.46).

His mother checks his blood sugar roughly every two hours, as well as before meals, to determine whether he needs insulin. Depending on Amir’s readings and what he eats, he may require two or three injections a day.

But the test strips needed for these checks have also become increasingly unaffordable, between 150 and 200 shekels ($45.87 to $61.17) for a box of 50. Before the war, Nahawand could buy two boxes for about 150 shekels ($45).

“Our children are already living with an illness,” she said. They should not have to suffer like this on top of it. Insulin is not too much to ask for.”

The International Diabetes Federation (IDF) said in August that it was “deeply concerned by the severe restrictions on access to insulin and essential diabetes care in Palestine”. It noted that access to diabetes care is particularly severely constrained in Gaza.

Awni Shweikh, executive director of the Haifa Association for Children with Diabetes, said her organisation speaks on behalf of about 800 children with diabetes in Gaza and appealed for urgent supplies of insulin pens and blood glucose testing strips.

Established in 2012 as the first association in Palestine dedicated to children with type 1 diabetes, Haifa used to provide a free box of testing strips every month to as many as 700 kids.

They also supplied insulin pens for children, offered educational sessions for families, provided psychological support and insulin to families not covered by UNRWA services. But since the start of the genocidal war in Gaza in October 2023, children lost their blood glucose monitoring devices and there was a severe shortage of insulin pens, threatening their lives.

“Insulin is not a luxury. It is a life-saving treatment,” Shweikh told Al Jazeera.

Some families have been forced to use expired insulin, resulting in kids being admitted to hospital with dangerously high blood sugar levels and complications involving acidity in the blood.

The loss of testing strips created a second, closely connected problem: even when parents managed to find insulin, they could not always measure their children’s blood sugar or determine the correct dose.

Afraid to eat

Alaa Ghaban, who lives with her family in a school for displaced Palestinians in Jabalia in northern Gaza, said insulin shortages have affected her daughter’s health and appetite.

Fifteen-year-old Janna was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes when she was just eight and needs two types of insulin, one taken during the day and another at night. Her thirty-six-year-old mother said she cannot stop either medication, but with supplies difficult to find and prices rising, securing both is a constant struggle.

One type of insulin that previously cost around 30 shekels ($9.17) now costs about 80 shekels ($24.46). But with no regular income, even reaching organisations that previously helped is becoming unaffordable.

Janna feared that eating without having enough insulin to control her blood sugar could be dangerous, so over the past four months, she has lost seven kilos.

“She has become afraid to eat because she is afraid she will wake up and not find insulin,” Alaa said.

Janna was recently admitted to hospital for eight days, malnourished and dehydrated, with tests showing high acidity levels in her blood and an enlarged liver.

Alaa once had to return to her family home under heavy Israeli bombardment to retrieve life-saving insulin for her daughter. Keeping medication cool is another daily challenge due to electricity shortages.

“My daughter sometimes wishes she were dead because she cannot bear watching us struggle and seeing me exhausted,” she said.

entries.title: US Congress helped end the Vietnam War. Can it stop the Iran war?
entries.summary: Congress forbade funding for the Vietnam War, contributing to the fall of the South Vietnamese government in Saigon.
entries.content:
Congress forbade funding for the Vietnam War, contributing to the fall of the South Vietnamese government in Saigon.

Democrats plan to force United States President Donald Trump to end the war on Iran as early as December although there’s worry their approach could trigger a government shutdown and pile on to soaring food and petrol prices.

Before this month’s midterm elections, the party promised to end the conflict, and its antiwar stance contributed to its sweeping wins at the polls as public anger has grown over the war.

After Democrats flipped multiple seats, including in deeply Republican strongholds, and seized majorities in both the Senate and House of Representatives, many lawmakers said they would refuse to pass new war appropriations once they take control of both chambers on January 3.

However, some in the party are preparing to use the “power of the purse” to stop US attacks even before the new Congress begins its work. They are eyeing a December 11 deadline by which Congress must pass a critical bill to extend funding for some federal agencies.

Here’s what we know:

What have Democratic senators said about ending the war?

Democrats have already tried multiple times through resolutions to end the US-Israel war on Iran without success.

In a joint statement last week, Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna called on Democratic lawmakers to leverage a funding deadline to ensure “not another cent of taxpayer money” goes to prolonging the conflict.

They were referring to a continuing funding package that Congress must deliberate on and pass by December 11. The package is meant to maintain government operations across defence and other sectors. The representatives said Congress should “oppose any funding package that does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations” in Iran.

Failure to pass the package would halt funding for federal agencies and trigger a government shutdown from December 12.

“The American people were loud and clear on November 3rd: they want an immediate end to Donald Trump’s reckless war in Iran,” they wrote in the open statement to their colleagues. “Passing such a measure would defy the demands of Americans who want this war to end – now.”

In an accompanying video, Khanna recalled that Congress ended the Vietnam War using the same approach.

Senator Chris Van Hollen, who is gunning for the Senate majority leader position in the new Congress, also said in a statement last week that any bills passed “must include language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran”.

Senators Tammy Duckworth, Michael Bennet and independent Bernie Sanders also signed the statement.

Did lawmakers force the end of the Vietnam War?

Indirectly, yes, by cutting off US financial support.

The 1955-1972 war was between communist North Vietnam and South Vietnam. The US supported the South and initially sent only military advisers and aid.

In 1964, a US Navy contingent positioned in the Gulf of Tonkin alleged direct attacks by North Vietnam. Congress thereafter passed a resolution granting President Lyndon B Johnson power to send troops without declaring war. The US deployed more than 500,000 soldiers and launched a scorched-earth bombardment.

But as the conflict dragged on and morale among US soldiers began to suffer amid high casualties, the war grew unpopular. Reports of US Army atrocities, including mass rape and massacres, further dampened public support. Congress repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in 1973 and ordered US forces to withdraw.

President Richard Nixon’s administration began handing over US military authority to South Vietnamese forces, but it also continued bombardments.

In June 1973, Congress passed the Case-Church Amendment, which forbade approved federal funding from going directly or indirectly to the war. More than two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers supported it, meaning Nixon could not override it with a presidential veto.

Lawmakers also passed the War Powers Resolution (or War Powers Act), which mandated that the president seek congressional approval before declaring war except in emergencies. Nixon vetoed it, but Congress overrode his veto in November 1973.

With US funding cut off, South Vietnam’s government in Saigon eventually fell in April 1975.

Are all Democrats willing to cut government funding?

The Trump administration irked Democrats when it failed to seek approval to declare war on Iran, a power that is constitutionally vested in Congress.

But not all Democrats support a government shutdown to end the war.

Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro, who in the new Congress will chair the influential House Appropriations Committee, which can block funding, told CBS News before the midterms that she would support “cutting off the funds” for the war.

However, she has not backed a shutdown and said she would rather approve a short-term funding extension rather than a funding package meant to run for a year.

“I think that the American people would like to see us end the war,” she told reporters on Wednesday. “I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war.”

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become speaker of the House in January, as well as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have not yet taken a stance.

Can the president use his veto power?

Yes, because Republicans still control Congress for another six weeks and Democrats, in the current Congress and the next, do not have the two-thirds majority required to override a presidential veto.

The two-thirds supermajority in the Senate requires 67 votes when all 100 senators participate. Even in the new Congress, in which Democrats will have a 56-44 majority, they will be 11 votes short.

Likewise, a two-thirds majority in the 435-member House requires 290 votes, but Democrats have secured 257 seats there in the next Congress.

In recent months despite not holding a majority, Democrats have forced more than 15 war powers votes in both chambers but have failed to pass them.

In September, seven House Republicans did vote with the Democrats in a bid to rebuke Trump, and the resolution passed 220-204.

However, Senate Republicans blocked it in a 51-48 vote last week.

Republicans, while admitting the high costs of the war, have argued the US needs to “finish the job”.

entries.title: Bruno Fernandes says contract talks on hold as Man United battle poor start
entries.summary: The Manchester United captain's current deal expires at the end of the season, though the club has an option to extend.
entries.content:
The Manchester United captain’s current deal expires at the end of the season, though the club has an option to extend.

Click here to join our live coverage of Liverpool against Manchester United.

Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes says the club has offered him a new contract, but discussions have ⁠been put on ⁠hold as the team focuses on turning around their poor form.

“Yeah, the club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay. And as you said, there are no negotiations going on,” Fernandes told Sky Sports in an interview published on ‌Sunday.

Fernandes’s current deal expires at the end of this season, although United ⁠hold an option to extend the midfielder’s contract by a further year until June 2028, giving the club more time to reach an agreement on new terms.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season; we came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but because of the context of the team and the club, I just put that to one side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations,” Fernandes said.

“The ⁠most important thing now is that the club gets ⁠back to winning games.”

The Portugal international also addressed comments claiming he had demanded more money and a longer deal, saying his priority was to remain at Old Trafford and help restore the ⁠club’s fortunes.

United are third from the bottom of the Premier League standings, having won only one of their opening 10 ⁠league matches, their worst start to a season ⁠in 40 years.

“I’ve seen people saying that he’s asked for more money; he’s asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here. I had somewhere to go to get ‌much more money than being at Manchester United,” Fernandes said.

“I could have been in a place that’s much warmer than Manchester.”

New manager Mauricio Pochettino, appointed after ‌Michael ‌Carrick was sacked earlier this month, will take charge of his first game when United face fifth-placed Liverpool on Sunday.

entries.title: Israeli settlers attack several Palestinian villages in occupied West Bank
entries.summary: Attacks in Ramallah, el-Bireh provinces included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on homes.
entries.content:
Attacks in Ramallah, el-Bireh provinces included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on homes.

Israeli settlers have attacked several Palestinian towns and villages in the central occupied West Bank, burning cars and damaging property.

The attacks early on Sunday included the burning of 12 vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on the walls of homes in Ramallah and el-Bireh provinces, reported the Palestinian news agency Wafa. The incidents were reported in Kafr Malik village, Deir Abu Mash’al village, and Deir al-Sudan village.

“Residents were awakened around two in the morning by sounds of fire and explosions. They realised the settlers had set fire to cars,” reported Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh from Kafr Malik.

Israeli settler violence has surged across the occupied West Bank since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza. At least 1,222 people, including 255 children, have been killed in attacks there since Israel launched its war in October 2023 in response to the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

The Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said there was a significant increase in the number of attacks throughout the Palestinian territory last month.

According to the Palestinian Authority body, there were 3,133 attacks in October, with Israeli forces responsible for 1,764 of them and Israeli settlers 1,369.

The commission said the total number of attacks increased by 53 percent compared with September when 2,051 attacks were recorded. Settler attacks alone rose from 647 in September to 1,369 in October – a 112 percent increase.

‘Jewish terrorism’

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar Party, who has been tasked with forming a new government after Israel’s general election last month, criticised the latest attacks on Sunday.

He wrote on social media that the attacks were “Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is”.

“Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives and severely damages the national security of the state of Israel and its foreign relations,” he posted on X.

“The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy,” he added, referring to far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

Ben-Gvir rejected the allegations and said Eisenkot was rushing to conclusions. He wrote on social media that Eisenkot’s stance represents a “down payment” to Arab Knesset member Ahmad Tibi in preparation for forming a government with the support of Arab parties.

Settlers are often “escorted by Israeli squads and they do nothing to stop the attackers,” Shai Parnes of the Israeli human rights organisation B’Tselem told Al Jazeera.

The Israeli military said it was sending police officers and investigators from the Criminal Identification Unit to the attacked areas “to collect evidence as part of the ongoing investigation”, the military wrote on social media.
